item.title: Centre says tribal leaders are not ‘necessary’ parties to Great Nicobar forest rights dispute
item.dc:creator: Simrin Sirur
item.author: Kundan Pandey
item.topic-tags: Forest Rights Act, Forests, Indigenous Peoples, Indigenous Rights, Islands, Land Rights, and Tribes
item.description:
- The Union Tribal Affairs Ministry has told the Calcutta High Court that Nicobarese leaders seeking to join a petition on Great Nicobar forest rights are “neither necessary nor proper parties,” and were “sleeping over” their rights during the statutory process.
- The Nicobarese petitioners allege that the 2022 forest rights settlement enabling the Island’s mega development project relied on consent from non-tribal settlers.
- Though the government maintains forest rights are settled, its own annual report shows zero claims settled in the Andaman and Nicobar Islands.
item.content:encoded: The Union Tribal Affairs Ministry has said that Nicobarese leaders seeking to join a petition challenging the settlement of forest rights on Great Nicobar Island are “neither necessary nor proper parties,” in the case, court documents show. The Nicobarese are one of two major tribes affected by the development of the Island, and primary claimants to forest rights in the area. An ongoing petition in the Calcutta High Court, filed by former IAS officer Meena Gupta, has challenged the Union government’s claim that rights under the Forest Rights Act (2005) (FRA) were settled on the Island. The FRA recognises the historical rights of tribal and other forest dwelling communities over forest resources, and makes compliance with its statutes necessary in clearing forest land for diversion. On July 9, 2026, four Nicobarese residents sought to join Gupta’s plea, arguing that government certifications claiming the settlement of forest rights was based on gram sabha consent from non-tribal settler communities. Apart from the Nicobarese and Shompen — a particularly vulnerable and largely uncontacted tribe — the Island is inhabited by families of ex-servicemen from the mainland who were settled on the remote Island from 1969 onwards as part of a state-sponsored scheme. “This certificate falsely states that the concerned Gram Sabhas have consented to the diversion of forest lands and cites meetings of the Gram Sabhas of the settler community in which no Nicobarese were present,” the impleadment document submitted to the court, seen by Mongabay-India, says. “No Gram Sabha meeting of the…This article was originally published on Mongabay

item.title: Farmers prepare for low rain but get floods instead
item.dc:creator: Sameeksha Sharma
item.author: Priyanka Shankar
item.topic-tags: Agriculture, Climate Change, Climate Change Adaptation, Extreme Weather Events, Food, Impacts of Climate Change, Monsoons, and Villages
item.description:
- Mahoba in Uttar Pradesh received 90% more rainfall than normal during the 2026 monsoon, flooding fields after farmers had prepared for a drier season based on forecasts of a strong El Niño.
- Tenant and small farmers face additional hurdles in accessing compensation, with land ownership, documentation and delayed claim processing affecting their access to insurance support.
- The widening gap between seasonal forecasts and localised weather events, makes it harder for farmers to plan according to the crop calendar.
item.content:encoded: “At the Krishi Vigyan Kendra in July, we were told to plant more sesame, groundnut and urad. These are crops expected to withstand less rain. But God decided to flood our fields instead,” shares Jaidevi, a farmer in Chandpura, a village in Mahoba, Uttar Pradesh, pointing to her withered sesame crop. Jaidevi and her husband own three bighas of farmland and have struggled to make a living from it. Chandpura is among the worst hit villages by intense rainfall in Mahoba during this southwest monsoon. Ahead of the 2026 southwest monsoon, Mahoba’s Krishi Vigyan Kendra advised farmers to sow low-water crops, anticipating low rainfall because of the effects of El Niño this year. The monsoon arrived nearly 20 days late, with deficient rainfall for much of the season that typically starts mid-June. But the pattern reversed in late August, when heavy rain lashed the region, leaving much of farmland waterlogged by September 15. This year’s El Niño forecast is expected to be one of the strongest on record. Its impact in India is in the form of a weaker monsoon and warmer temperatures. In June, the agriculture ministry classified Mahoba as one of 111 high-priority districts based on irrigation coverage and vulnerability to rainfall deficits. Irrigation coverage in these districts is expected to be below 25 percent. Part of the drought-prone Bundelkhand region, Mahoba has long faced rainfall deficits, falling groundwater levels and limited irrigation. item.description: Nepal, which suffered a catastrophic debris flow and flash flood on August 26, is slated to receive $21.6 million from the United Nations’ Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage (FRLD). The decision to “provisionally” release the funds was finalised during an “extraordinary meeting” convened by the Fund’s board on October 22. Nepal will still […]
item.content:encoded: Nepal, which suffered a catastrophic debris flow and flash flood on August 26, is slated to receive $21.6 million from the United Nations’ Fund for Responding to Loss and Damage (FRLD). The decision to “provisionally” release the funds was finalised during an “extraordinary meeting” convened by the Fund’s board on October 22. Nepal will still need to apply for this funding, and the Board will consider the request at its next meeting, the tenth FRLD Board meeting, this December. “Following Nepal’s formal letter on August 31, 2026 requesting support from the Fund, the FRLD Board commenced to assess available options. Backed by strong solidarity from the whole Board, intensive consultations were held throughout September and October, culminating in today’s extraordinary Board meeting, in accordance with the Board’s Rules of Procedure,” an FRLD press statement said. The FRLD was constituted in 2023 with the specific purpose of providing rapid financial support to developing countries struggling with the economic and non-economic losses and damages associated with climate-driven extreme weather events. The demand by developing countries for a funding facility for losses and damages had been simmering at the climate Conference of Parties (COP) meetings for decades. The decision to provisionally release funding to Nepal comes ahead of the COP31 in Antalya, Türkiye, scheduled to take place from November 9 to November 20. Climate change was “a destabilising factor” in the Nepal flash flood, according to a report by the World Weather Attribution. item.title: The Sundarbans at the crossroads of climate change and human survival [Commentary]
item.dc:creator: C.P. Rajendran
item.author: Aditi Tandon
item.locations: Bay of Bengal, Global, and West Bengal
item.topic-tags: Agriculture, Biodiversity, Climate Change, Ecology, Environment, Extreme Weather Events, Floods, Forests, Global Warming, Impacts of Climate Change, Mangroves, Rivers, Salinisation, Sea Level Rise, Villages, Wetlands, and Wildlife
item.description:
- The Indian Sundarbans has become a major source of climate-induced displacement and distress migration in India.
- The Amphibious Living Opportunities approach offers a path forward by combining resilient housing, diversified climate-adapted livelihoods, and community-driven initiatives.
- The framework’s success will depend on sustained investment, institutional commitment, and the active participation of the communities most at risk.
- The views in this commentary are those of the author.
item.content:encoded: Spanning India and Bangladesh, with India comprising 40% of its area, a vast and ever-shifting mangrove forest stretches across the Bay of Bengal. This vast delta derives its name from the Sundari (Heritiera fomes), the tall mangrove species that flourishes here in abundance. The name “Sundarbans” is a modern rendering of “Sunderbunds,” a term coined by Walter Hamilton in the East India Gazetteer, meaning “Forests of the Soondry” (“Sundri,” or beautiful). Heritiera fomes is the abundant tall mangrove species of the region. Where the rivers Ganga (Padma in Bangladesh), Brahmaputra, and Meghna discharge into the Bay of Bengal, they form the Sundarbans — the largest contiguous mangrove forest on Earth. Toward the coast, the forest transitions into a low-lying swamp of sand dunes, mud flats, and barren expanses, intersected by innumerable tidal streams and channels. Four protected areas within this remarkable landscape are recognised as UNESCO World Heritage Sites: Sundarbans West, South, and East in Bangladesh, and Sundarbans National Park in India. The nutrient-rich mangrove waters of India’s eastern coast form a vital breeding ground and nursery for roughly 90% of the region’s aquatic species. The ecosystem is notable for supporting overlapping populations of threatened aquatic mammals, including the Ganges river dolphin and the Irrawaddy dolphin. This extraordinary species concentration in the Sundarbans stems from the dynamic mixing of freshwater from major rivers — the Ganga and the Brahmaputra among them — with the saltwater of the Bay of Bengal. item.title: Community models could help conserve the disappearing migratory freshwater fish [Commentary]
item.dc:creator: Saurabh Dewan
item.author: Priyanka Shankar
item.topic-tags: Extinction, Fish, Himalayas, Mountains, Rivers, and Wildlife
item.description:
- Migratory freshwater fish have declined by 81% globally since the 1970s, with the Ganges-Brahmaputra-Meghna basin as a critical migration landscape where river giants like the golden mahseer are quietly disappearing.
- As riverbed habitats are disappearing with the impacts of climate change, impassable hydropower dams like Tehri and Srinagar are trapping fish into small, inbred, genetic islands.
- Decentralised, local stewardship can successfully restore wild fish populations while sustaining river livelihoods.
- The views in the commentary are that of the author.
item.content:encoded: When the United Nations Convention on the Conservation of Migratory Species of Wild Animals (CMS) published its Global Assessment of Migratory Freshwater Fishes report earlier this year, the numbers confirmed what riverine communities had suspected for decades. Migratory freshwater fish populations have dropped 81% globally since the 1970s. Nearly all (97%) of the 58 fish species listed under the convention now face extinction. The report, drafted in collaboration with the UN Environment Programme-World Conservation Monitoring Centre (UNEP-WCMC) names the Ganges-Brahmaputra-Meghna (GBM) river system as a global priority region. Zeb Hogan, a fish biologist and one of the report’s lead authors, describes the GBM basin as among South Asia’s greatest migration landscapes. It is a single connected pathway from Himalayan headwaters down to the Bay of Bengal. Yet, despite supporting an immense biomass of migratory species, the basin is collapsing under severe habitat fragmentation driven by aggressive hydropower expansion and altered flow regimes. Public debate about the GBM usually stops at the lower reaches, majorly at barrages like Farakka. The damage is worse far above the plains. In the high-altitude headwaters of the Indian Himalayan Region, the lifelines that flow-dependent species depend on are being cut apart piece by piece. Cascading hazards and the dislocation of aquatic life In late August 2026, a massive ice and rock avalanche struck the Nepal-Tibet border. The debris tore into the Lende Khola before surging down the Bhote Koshi and Trishuli rivers. item.title: Cloud seeding’s potential to ease drought is uncertain
item.dc:creator: Nikhil Sreekandan
item.author: Aditi Tandon
item.topic-tags: Cities and Towns, Climate Change, Climate Change Adaptation, Climate Science, Drought, Extreme Weather Events, and Water
item.description:
- Karnataka recorded a 35% rainfall deficit between June 1 and September 30, 2026.
- The government launched a 60-day cloud-seeding programme to address the state’s rainfall deficit, despite warnings of unfavourable conditions.
- Weather experts have called for caution, noting that there may be too few rain-bearing clouds to seed. They also raise concerns about limited public communication on this effort.
item.content:encoded: The Karnataka government launched a cloud-seeding programme in September to address rainfall deficits in drought-affected parts of the state. Since the launch of the programme, worth around ₹28 crore (₹285 million), questions have been raised about the viability of cloud-seeding operations this late in the monsoon. Cloud seeding is a disputed weather modification technique that introduces particles into suitable existing clouds to influence how precipitation forms. It cannot create new clouds, and its effect on rainfall is difficult to measure. Weather experts, including senior IMD officials, have cautioned that “conditions are not favourable” for cloud seeding in Karnataka. Highest rainfall deficit on record “For the people of Karnataka, drought is a very common feature,” says G.S. Srinivasa Reddy, former director of the Karnataka State Natural Disaster Monitoring Centre (KSNDMC), who has 35 years of experience in real-time weather monitoring. Since the turn of the 21st century, Reddy says, 17 of the 26 years have been drought years in Karnataka. But 2026 has been particularly severe, as the state recorded just 551 millimetres of rainfall between June 1 and September 30, a record 35% rainfall deficit. According to the KSNDMC, 30 districts and 209 taluks in the state recorded rainfall ranging from “deficit” to “large deficit” in the June to September period. The India Meteorological Department (IMD) forecast notes that 2026 will be an El Niño year, and, according to Reddy, almost 60% of Karnataka’s drought years have coincided with El Niño. item.title: The toxic tyre chemical no one is measuring
item.dc:creator: Lakshmi Nilakantan
item.author: Kundan Pandey
item.topic-tags: Cities and Towns, Environment, Fish, Industry, Pollution, Rivers, Roads, and Water Pollution
item.description:
- A chemical used to make tyres last longer turns into 6PPD-quinone, a toxin linked to mass deaths of salmon in the U.S.
- With vehicle and tyre sales rising in India, experts warn the problem could grow, but no data exists on the toxin’s levels in Indian road dust, stormwater or water bodies.
- Experts call for regulating 6PPD and better stormwater management, as poor drainage and sewage-laden storm drains in Indian cities could carry the toxin into water bodies.
item.content:encoded: Every time a vehicle moves, its tyres shed tiny particles. Some of these particles carry a chemical that, in the U.S., was found killing salmon in urban streams after rain. India is selling more vehicles than ever before, yet experts say there is no data on how much of this chemical reaches the country’s rivers. The chemical is 6PPD (N-(1,3-dimethylbutyl)-N′-phenyl-p-phenylenediamine), an additive used worldwide to increase tyre durability. It became a concern after researchers from the U.S. published a study in the journal Science in December 2020, linking a compound formed from 6PPD to mass deaths of coho salmon in urban streams after rain. “6PPD is used to neutralise ozone, prevent cracks in the rubber, and extend the lifespan of the tyre,” according to a January review article in RSC Advances by the Royal Society of Chemistry. The review opens by noting that India’s tyre market is expanding with its automotive industry, then examines the toxic effects of 6PPD-quinone (6PPD-Q), a byproduct formed when 6PPD reacts with ozone. Echoing the same, Paul Sharp, a chemist and Professor Emeritus, University of Missouri, Columbia, USA, says, “6PPD-Q is the ozonisation byproduct of 6PPD and formed as a tyre wear particle. It has no boundaries and is ubiquitous all over the motorised world. These can make their way into water bodies during rainstorms, leading to rapid/mass death of aquatic species.” Responding to Mongabay-India’s email interview, Sharp explains that as tyres wear down, 6PPD reacts with ground-level ozone to form 6PPD-Q. item.title: How Columbus’ voyages accelerated the homogenisation of Earth’s biodiversity [Commentary]
item.dc:creator: R.J. Ranjit Daniels
item.author: Arathimenon
item.topic-tags: Animals, Biodiversity, Conservation, Ecology, and Extinction
item.description:
- Columbus’ arrival in the New World ushered in global biogeographical shifts and ecological disruption, weakening the resilience of the biosphere.
- His voyages set in motion an unprecedented exchange of biodiversity across geographical boundaries.
- Introduced microorganisms, plants and animals spread to new regions, with some becoming invasive or causing epidemics, contributing to biogeographical homogenisation.
- The views in this commentary are that of the author.
item.content:encoded: Christopher Columbus was a legendary 15th-century Italian explorer whose “misadventures” opened the way for large-scale biogeographical homogenisation. Over the past 500 years, since Columbus first sailed west across the Atlantic Ocean to reach the “New World”, Earth has witnessed unprecedented cross-boundary human movement and the exchange of living organisms. These movements have brought about major shifts in the geographical distribution of microorganisms, plants and animals. While thousands of introduced plants and animals have acquired the deplorable status of “invasive alien species”, introduced pathogenic microorganisms, such as those that cause smallpox, cholera, sexually transmitted diseases and plague, have been major culprits in wiping out indigenous human populations and cultures across the world. History has also shown that introduced phytopathogenic microorganisms have devastated agriculture, causing widespread famine and human suffering. The post-Columbus transformation of Earth’s biogeography has proved catastrophic. In 1995, when UNESCO celebrated the silver jubilee of its Man and the Biosphere Programme, the event was held in Seville, Spain, where Columbus was laid to rest. The choice of venue could have hinted at Columbus’ unintentional contribution to the ecological chaos that Earth has witnessed over the past 500 years. Biogeographical periods shaping the biosphere Biogeography is the science that seeks to understand the patterns of geographical distribution of organisms and the reasons behind them, as well as the ecosystems in which organisms develop and coexist. item.title: New study maps India’s diverging fire regimes
item.dc:creator: Simrin Sirur
item.author: Kundan Pandey
item.topic-tags: Conservation, Fires, Forest Fires, and Forests
item.description: New research from the Centre for Wildlife Studies evaluated changing fire regimes in wildlife reserves across three Indian landscapes, finding that burned area rose most steeply in the Eastern Ghats between 2002 and 2022, at 9.3% per year. The rising fires in the Eastern Ghats show that it has a more fire-prone combination of vegetation, […]
item.content:encoded: New research from the Centre for Wildlife Studies evaluated changing fire regimes in wildlife reserves across three Indian landscapes, finding that burned area rose most steeply in the Eastern Ghats between 2002 and 2022, at 9.3% per year. The rising fires in the Eastern Ghats show that it has a more fire-prone combination of vegetation, climate, and repeated human ignition than the Western Ghats, while Central India sits in between. The study evaluated roughly 20,000 square kilometres of protected forest land across 13 reserves. Both human and climate factors explained between 21 and 77% of annual fire activity across individual reserves, with drought and community fire use both playing major, but regionally varying roles. A region- and reserve-specific deconstruction of forest fires is essential to understanding how different rainfall, temperature, and land use regimes, as well as population densities, affect fire occurrence, the researchers argue. For example, high human population density was strongly associated with more frequent fires in Kawal Wildlife Sanctuary (Telangana) and Nagarjunasagar-Srisailam Tiger Reserve (Andhra Pradesh), but in Nagarahole and Bandipur National Parks (Karnataka), similar conditions were linked with fewer fires. “Various factors could be contributing to this paradoxical trend in burned areas in India, including forest management, land-use change, changes in fire ignitions, anthropogenic climate change and natural climate variability,” the study says. Using satellite-derived burned-area data from NASA’s MODIS sensor, the study found that burned area in the Western Ghats declined by 10.8% per year. item.title: The endurance runner of the grasslands
item.dc:creator: Team Mongabay-India
item.author: Priyanka Shankar
item.topic-tags: Biodiversity, Conservation, Ecology, Grasslands, Mammals, and Wildlife
item.description: A creature of the open grasslands, the blackbuck’s evolutionary survival trick is endurance — it can sprint incredibly fast.
item.content:encoded: Species File: Exploring India’s biodiversity, one species at a time. A creature of the open grasslands, where there’s nowhere to hide, the blackbuck’s evolutionary survival trick is endurance — it can sprint incredibly fast, sometimes even fast enough to have once outrun the Asiatic cheetah when it still prevailed in India. The blackbuck (Antilope cervicapra) is the sole living member of its genus. In a 2025 story published in Mongabay-India, Mihir Godbole, founder of The Grasslands Trust-India, said: “Blackbucks … are key indicators that grassland species cannot do well in any other habitats.” Female blackbucks are light brown and live in herds, sometimes led by a mature male. Younger males live in bachelor groups until they mature, at which point they establish their own territories, develop a black-brown coat, and grow corkscrewed horns. During mating season, males form display territories called leks, leaping and calling to attract females. Once spread across the Indian subcontinent, blackbuck populations were decimated by trophy hunting under British rule. The species is now extinct in the wild in Pakistan and Bangladesh and survives in small protected pockets in Nepal, while the majority live in India. A 2016 estimate put the Indian population at roughly 35,000. They live in the open grassland habitats and are found across 13 states, with strongholds in Velavadar, Tal Chhapar, Point Calimere, and Karnataka’s Ranebennur and Jayamangali reserves. The IUCN lists the blackbuck as least concern, indicating that its population is widespread and abundant. In India, it’s protected under Schedule I…This article was originally published on Mongabay

item.title: India’s new climate targets must navigate geopolitical uncertainty [Commentary]
item.dc:creator: Pallavi DasVaibhav Chaturvedi
item.author: Kundan Pandey
item.topic-tags: Clean Energy, Climate Change, Climate Change Adaptation, Climate Change Mitigation, Environment, Environmental Economics, Fossil Fuels, Global Warming, Green Energy, Greenhouse Gas Emissions, Impacts of Climate Change, Oil, and Renewable Energy
item.description:
- India’s updated Nationally Determined Contribution targets 60% non-fossil power capacity by 2035.
- Studies suggest India’s non-fossil fuel capacity could reach 60-68% by 2035, depending on economic growth, demand-side savings, and the cost of solar panels.
- High oil and gas prices could speed up electrification and strengthen the case for clean power capacity.
- The views in the commentary are those of the authors.
item.content:encoded: Well past the summer peak, India’s power system remains under strain. The country met daytime demand of over 267 GW even in September, yet fell short by more than 7.7 GW after sunset, when solar generation tapers off. India may have withdrawn its bid to host COP33 in 2028, but COP31, which opens in Antalya on November 9, will be the first UN climate summit since India submitted its 2035 Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC). It raises the bar for climate ambition, targeting 60% non-fossil installed capacity by 2035 and relying heavily on the power sector to drive the transition over the next decade. Climate impacts are rising in India and worldwide. The world will likely cross the 1.5°C threshold in the next few years, as per a recent UN Environment Programme (UNEP) report. The margin by which this threshold is breached before accelerated mitigation efforts bend the temperature curve again will determine how catastrophic climate impacts become. All countries must double down on mitigation now. Yet India’s 2035 NDC targets are being tested in real time, as rising demand, especially in non-solar hours, pushes for all available options, including fossil energy. At the same time, annual power demand could still be hit if India’s economic growth slows because of global conflict, trade disputes, supply chain concentrations, energy inflation, and the impact of artificial intelligence. The clean energy transition risks losing momentum just as it needs to accelerate. A target built for uncertainty India’s current position reflects both progress and credibility.…This article was originally published on Mongabay

item.title: New-to-science seahorse is one of three long-misidentified species
item.dc:creator: Ananya Singh
item.author: Priyanka Shankar
item.topic-tags: Biodiversity, Coast, Conservation, Ecology, Fish, New species, Oceans, Wildlife, and Wildlife Trade
item.description:
- Scientists have identified a new seahorse species, Hippocampus amandavincentae, from the Indian Ocean, based on two specimens collected from trawler bycatch in Tamil Nadu.
- The discovery has helped resolve over a century of taxonomic misidentification by revealing that the thorny seahorse, earlier believed to be a single species – Hippocampus histrix, is actually three distinct species.
- As indiscriminate fishing and illegal trade threaten seahorse populations, the study’s findings contribute to a clearer picture of spiny seahorse diversity in the Indo-Pacific region.
item.content:encoded: Scientists have identified a new-to-science seahorse species from the Indian waters, which has helped resolve the taxonomy of a group misidentified for over a century. In 1856, zoologist Johann Jakob Kaup described the thorny or spiny seahorse, Hippocampus histrix, based on samples from Japan. Since then, this seahorse has been thought to be a single, widespread species ranging from the Red Sea, through the Indian Ocean to Japan, Indonesia and the Pacific Islands. Over 150 years later, in 2019, a team of researchers collected two seahorse specimens from trawler bycatch that landed at the Thoothukudi Fisheries Harbour in Tamil Nadu. After studying their morphology and genetic data, and comparing them with samples housed in museum collections around the world, the researchers realised that these two specimens represented a distinct lineage. Their study, published recently in Zootaxa, confirmed what was once thought to be H. histrix is not one, but three separate species—Hippocampus histrix in the Pacific Ocean, Hippocampus jayakari in the Arabian region, and the newly described species from the Indian Ocean named Hippocampus amandavincentae, whose population had long been clubbed with H. histrix. The findings provide a better understanding of spiny seahorse diversity in the Indo-Pacific region. “This discovery shows that identification and understanding species is the first step towards protecting them and their habitat,” said Shalu Kannan, the study’s lead author and a project scientist at the Zoological Survey of India, Andaman and Nicobar Regional Centre. item.title: One orangutan goes home. Will the five babies follow?
item.dc:creator: Arathi Menon
item.author: Aditi Tandon
item.topic-tags: Biodiversity, Conservation, Endangered species, Mammals, Pet Trade, Primates, Wildlife, Wildlife Trade, Wildlife Trafficking, and Zoos
item.description:
- An orangutan seized from a Mumbai apartment in 2024 is being repatriated to Indonesia after two years of delays over health and procedural issues.
- The juvenile will be sent to a rehabilitation centre in Sumatra, where experts say he could be prepared for release into the wild in a few years.
- Indonesia is also seeking the repatriation of five baby orangutans rescued in Odisha, whose origins and suspected trafficking are under investigation.
item.content:encoded: Two years since an infant orangutan was seized from a Mumbai apartment, the procedures are finally complete to repatriate him to his homeland, Indonesia. The animal will fly out of India on October 19, 2026, after a long bilateral process, delayed by procedural hurdles and poor health condition of the animal, according to Yogesh Nilkand Warkad, the assistant management authority of CITES, Mumbai, who is overseeing the operation in India. In the meantime, the infant orangutan, who was estimated to be around one year at the time of seizure from a private apartment in Dombivli, Mumbai, was transferred to Gorewada zoo in Maharashtra in consultation with the then Chief Wildlife Warden Vivek Khandekar, Warkad informs. Then, due to poor health from a respiratory issue when he was just one and a half years of age, he was transferred to Vantara zoo in Gujarat, for subsequent rehabilitation. He was recuperating there, as per the authorities. “This is the first successful repatriation of a seized CITES animal from India and my office (Asst. Management Authority CITES) did everything in our capacity to make it happen,” Warkad informs Mongabay-India over the phone. Mongabay-India has previously reported on the increasing smuggling of non-human primates, particularly apes, into India, primarily by air from Southeast Asian countries such as Malaysia. Beyond violating CITES regulations, the trade threatens already critically endangered species such as orangutans with further population declines in their native habitats. It also raises serious ethical concerns, given the complex social bonds of these animals…This article was originally published on Mongabay

item.title: Small-scale fisheries a big threat to rays
item.dc:creator: Rupsy Khurana
item.author: Aditi Tandon
item.topic-tags: Biodiversity, Coast, Conservation, Ecology, Endangered species, Environment, Environmental Politics, Fish, Fishing, Natural Resources, Oceans, Wildlife, Wildlife Protection Act, and Wildlife Trade
item.description:
- A study documenting manta and devil ray landings across a decade in a coastal area in Tamil Nadu reveals declining populations and fewer adult rays.
- The proportion of adult spinetail devil rays in marine species brought to shore fell from 64% to 26% over the study period. With rays producing just one pup every two to three years, the loss of breeding adults makes population recovery more difficult.
- Though all 10 species of manta and devil rays were listed under CITES Appendix I in November 2025, prohibiting commercial international trade, the restrictions do not cover domestic catches and trade.
item.content:encoded: Manta and devil rays, collectively known as mobulids, are large cartilaginous fish known for their broad, wing-like pectoral fins, which help them glide through the water. They often feed on zooplankton and small crustaceans and fish in shallow coastal waters, making them vulnerable to entanglement in fishing nets. Roughly 259,000 mobulids are killed each year in fisheries, globally. Five countries — India, Indonesia, Sri Lanka, Myanmar and Peru — account for 87% of these deaths, which are mostly attributed to small-scale fisheries. India is the highest contributor, accounting for 28.2% deaths. Limited catch data and inadequate understanding of the impacts of small-scale fisheries make it difficult to assess the status of these species. Increasing fishing pressure puts several ray species at risk of population collapse. To address this gap, a group of researchers tracked mobulid bycatch from fishing boats in Thoothukudi, Tamil Nadu, between 2013 and 2023. Their study, published in Conservation Science and Practice, found evidence of declining populations of four species — the spinetail devil ray (Mobula mobular), the sicklefin devil ray (Mobula tarapacana), the oceanic manta ray (Mobula birostris), and the bentfin devil ray (Mobula thurstoni). The study notes that these population declines occurred alongside increasing fishing pressure, suggesting overfishing as the likely cause. “Counting the number of mobula rays caught is always confusing,” said Divya Karnad, a senior lecturer at the University of Exeter and an author of the study. item.title: Two new-to-science subterranean fishes reveal a hidden world underneath
item.dc:creator: Monish Upadhyay
item.author: Priyanka Shankar
item.reporting-project: Almost Famous Species and Beyond Protected Areas
item.topic-tags: Biodiversity, Conservation, Ecology, Fish, Groundwater, New species, Positive Environmental, Research, Villages, Water, and Wildlife
item.description:
- Researchers have described two new subterranean species, Gitchak nakana (a transparent, blind loach) and Rakthamichthys anchi (a transparent, blind swamp eel), from wells in Assam.
- Deeper groundwater systems in Assam and northeast India are only partially mapped and remain poorly understood beyond 200 m depth, experts say.
- Any impacts observed on surface water percolate into the groundwater impacting subterranean species. Therefore, it is crucial to monitor habitats and keep a check on pollution, researchers warn.
item.content:encoded: A decade ago, Wimarithy K. Marak, a resident of Assam’s Goalpara district, often used to encounter a small pink creature in her neighbourhood’s wells. She simply thought of it as a worm infesting her locality. In 2021, after she became a researcher, she stumbled upon the creature again while drawing water from a well. “This time I sent the picture to my supervisor and we brought a specimen to the lab,” she says. The creature turned out to be a two-centimetre long blind loach with a body so transparent that its blood and internal organs give it a striking blood-red appearance. The first specimen was collected in March 2021. Although further explorations into neighbouring wells yielded no results for the now described Gitchak nakana, the team of researchers had requested village residents to alert Marak if they came across anything unusual in their wells. Much later in 2024, when one of Marak’s relatives was cleaning his well, he came across what seemed like a worm. “My relatives had fully drained the well and that is when they found a  specimen of another subterranean species,” she says. Named Rakthamichthys anchi, the holotype, measuring around 310 mm, was collected in May 2024. R. anchi is a slender eel-like fish which shares characteristics with Gitchak nakana. Researchers then published two papers earlier this year describing both the species. item.title: As the Ganga treaty nears expiry, renewed concerns over water sharing arise
item.dc:creator: Umesh Kumar Ray
item.author: Kundan Pandey
item.topic-tags: Cities and Towns, Drought, Environment, Environmental Politics, Rivers, and Water
item.description:
- As the Ganga Water Sharing Treaty with Bangladesh nears renewal, Bihar wants to resolve its demand for a fixed share of Ganga water during the lean period first.
- Experts do not buy Bihar’s claim that the treaty burdens the state. They say the real issue is siltation caused by the Farakka barrage.
- Experts suggest Bihar made a stakeholder and that its concerns over water availability, siltation and erosion can be addressed through a basin-wide approach.
item.content:encoded: As the Ganga water-sharing treaty between India and Bangladesh ends this year, Bihar seeks to resolve its long-standing demands before the treaty is renewed. The treaty, signed in December 1996, governs the sharing of the Ganga river’s water between upstream India and downstream Bangladesh, particularly during the lean season when river flows are low. Under the treaty, during the lean period from January to June, if water at the Farakka barrage is less than 70,000 cubic feet per second (cusecs), India and Bangladesh each get half. If the water at the barrage is between 70,000 and 75,000 cusecs, Bangladesh will be assured 35,000 cusecs, and the rest will go to India. If the water is 75,000 cusecs or more, India will get an assured 40,000 cusecs, and Bangladesh will get the rest. The agreement further says Bangladesh will get a guaranteed flow of 35,000 cusecs on the first and last ten days of April and 27,633 cusecs between April 11 and 20. If the Ganga’s flow falls below 50,000 cusecs in any ten-day period, the two governments will enter immediate consultations to make emergency adjustments. For decades, Bihar’s political leaders have argued that the Ganga water-sharing treaty with Bangladesh does not adequately account for the state’s water needs. Sanjay Jha, a member of parliament from Bihar’s ruling party Janata Dal United, said on August 6 during the Zero Hour in Rajya Sabha that renewing the treaty without adequately incorporating Bihar’s long-term water security, development needs, and water resource requirements would…This article was originally published on Mongabay

item.title: Light may influence morning basking behaviour in captive gharials
item.dc:creator: Lekha Bandopadhyay
item.author: Arathimenon
item.reporting-project: Almost Famous Species and Beyond Protected Areas
item.topic-tags: Animal Behaviour, Animals, Biodiversity, Conservation, Ecology, Encroachment, Endangered species, Endemic species, Environment, Protected Areas, Reptiles, Rivers, and Wildlife
item.description:
- A study on captive gharials suggests light could be a stronger cue than temperature for morning basking movements, particularly among young gharials.
- Researchers call for studies on wild gharials to understand how light affects basking behaviour.
- With a species recovery score of just 19%, habitat protection remains crucial for both wild gharials and captive-reared individuals reintroduced into rivers.
item.content:encoded: Like all crocodilians, Gangetic gharials regulate their body temperature using external heat sources. They warm their enormous bodies, which can grow to 15 to 20 feet in length, by basking on sandbanks, making it an important daily activity. Both temperature and light are important environmental cues for basking. However, a recent study on captive Gangetic gharials (Gavialis gangeticus) finds that light is a stronger cue than temperature for their morning basking movements. The researchers expected natural light to be a reliable indicator for gharials to determine the right time to bask on land, says Megha Khanduri, the study’s lead author and a postdoctoral researcher at the University of Helsinki, Finland. However, artificial lighting at night and the resulting light pollution can disrupt the relationship between natural light and temperature in the environment. The study finds that if light is the more dominant cue for basking, this disruption could lead gharials to bask at the wrong time, when air temperatures are not warm enough, or choose suboptimal basking sites. “Such behaviours could be potentially life-threatening as it can result in hypothermia,” says Khanduri. “If hatchlings leave the water earlier than the adults because of differences in sensitivity to light, it could also expose them to terrestrial predators in the early hours.” Radiant cue for basking The study was conducted on 382 captive gharials raised from eggs and housed in enclosures at the Deori EcoCentre in Madhya Pradesh. item.content:encoded: Are invasive plants better at competing with species in places they invade than species in their native range? A paper investigated this using Erigeron canadensis, commonly known as Canadian horseweed, to find that plants from non-native populations had 19.2% higher competitive ability than those from native populations. In the study, that advantage was evident across two watering conditions — watered and drought. Although drought reduced competitive ability overall by 12.9%, the difference between native and non-native populations was not significant. Canadian horseweed is native to North and Central America that has spread widely across Europe, Asia and other regions. In some introduced areas, it can suppress other plant species and reduce local plant diversity. The researchers conducted a large glasshouse experiment involving plants from 100 native and 165 non-native populations of Erigeron canadensis. They grew the plants under different conditions, including adequate water and drought, and tested how they performed when growing alone, alongside individuals of their own species, and alongside other plant species. The paper suggests that the competitive advantage evolved independently in different regions. Genetic analyses identified four clusters, but increased competitive ability was evident in two. The result suggests that similar evolutionary changes can emerge independently rather than being explained solely by the spread of one already competitive lineage. One of the crucial findings was that the advantage was associated with interactions with other species, rather than competition between individuals of the same species. item.title: Noise pollution is a public health risk that’s hard to measure and monitor
item.dc:creator: Disha Shetty
item.author: Aditi Tandon
item.topic-tags: Cities and Towns, Environment, Environmental Politics, Health impacts, Human Rights, and Pollution
item.description:
- Noise pollution is an environmental stressor linked to health impacts.
- Large-scale measurement of noise pollution is difficult due to the nature of sound and limited access to acoustic models, leaving gaps in data on noise in Indian cities.
- In some cities, citizen groups have been demanding action against noise pollution, building political pressure. Enforcement of rules is key to progress, say activists.
item.content:encoded: A recent debate over using DJs and high-powered sound systems during Pune’s Ganesh festival brought noise pollution and its health impacts into focus. In August and September, residents and citizen groups in Pune called for stricter enforcement of noise limit rules, prompting a parliamentary committee review of noise and light pollution. The National Human Rights Commission also sought a report from Maharashtra’s pollution control board on action taken on noise limit violations during the festival. The impact of urban noise extends beyond festivals. Prolonged exposure to environmental noise is linked to sleep disturbance, hearing impairment and cardiovascular risks, making noise pollution a public health concern in India’s increasingly noisy cities. Gaps in noise pollution data from Indian cities and the challenges of monitoring sound levels at scale are compounding the problem, say researchers. Meanwhile, citizens have been pushing for better policy and better implementation of guidelines, with incremental changes being observed over the years, say noise pollution activists. Under-researched “silent killer” “It’s been known for a long time that noise is more than just a nuisance or an annoyance, but that it’s a serious cardiovascular disease concern,” said Danielle Vienneau, Associate Professor at the UMC Utrecht in The Netherlands, an expert on environmental pollution and its impact on human health. item.content:encoded: On October 11, the Upper Siang district administration issued an order prohibiting the assembly of five or more people amid intensifying protests against the Siang Upper Multipurpose Project (SUMP). The order was issued two days after four protesters were detained under the Arunachal Pradesh Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act, 2014. Protests against the 11,000 MW hydropower plant turned violent earlier this month after Chief Minister Pema Khandu’s visit to the district. Residents of the Siang, Upper Siang, and East Siang districts have consistently opposed the development of the dam, which will submerge 27 villages, including Upper Siang’s district headquarters, Yingkiong. On October 13, three civil society groups — the Adi Banne Kebang United, Siang Indigenous Farmers Forum Youth Wing, and SUMP Affected Area Youth Association (SAAYA) submitted a memorandum to the Upper Siang District Collector condemning police atrocities and demanding the immediate release of those arrested for protesting. Police allegedly lathi charged protesters on October 4, days after protesters set fire to vehicles and stormed an MLA’s house. The memorandum demands the unconditional release of protesters from police custody, the “immediate and complete withdrawal of Central Armed Police Forces from Siang and Upper Siang,” a halt on all studies being done to determine the dam’s viability in the area, and the quashing of all legal proceedings against protesters. “Failure to comply will compel the youth and public to escalate democratic agitation, for which the district administration and law enforcement authorities shall be held solely responsible,” says the memorandum, seen by Mongabay-India.…This article was originally published on Mongabay
